claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is single-phase fcc.
Additive manufacturing produces a high intrinsic density of edge dislocations in Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
Processing-induced edge dislocations act as preferential sites for oxide nucleation and growth during high-temperature exposure.
Dislocation cores and their strain fields provide enhanced diffusion pathways for ingress of oxygen or reducing-gas species.
Enhanced transport along dislocations is the primary factor governing degradation of this alloy.
A high dislocation density accelerates oxide-scale formation and growth.
A post-processing heat treatment can reduce dislocation density while preserving composition and the fcc structure.
Reducing dislocation density should remove preferential transport pathways and slow oxidation.
High-dislocation-density specimens will oxidize faster than heat-treated, low-dislocation-density specimens.
High-dislocation-density specimens will exhibit greater mass gain.
High-dislocation-density specimens will form thicker and more continuous oxide scales.
The predicted dislocation-density effect will occur in both oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
The degradation mechanism can operate without inducing a transformation away from the fcc matrix.
Avoiding a phase transformation will preserve the alloy's mechanical performance during exposure.
The as-built target alloy has demonstrated high strength and fatigue performance.
Intrinsic edge dislocations introduced by additive manufacturing can enhance elevated-temperature strain hardening and deformability.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 900–1000 °C while the alloy remains single-phase fcc.
Failure to observe a statistically significant association between dislocation density and degradation would falsify the proposed primary-governor mechanism.
